The life cycle of a frog also has four stages.
Stage 1 : Frogs lay hundreds of eges at a time in a pond or lake. A jelly-like covering protects each eggs. the
eggs appear like a white jelly-like substance floating in water. This floating cluster of frog’s eggs is called a frog
spawn. The eggs reach the embryaq stage in 3-4 days.

Stage 2 : When an egg hatches, a ta pole come out. It has a tail, no legs, and gills to breathe in water. After
about 5 weeks, the tadpole begins to grow legs. First the front legs appear, then the back legs.
Stage 3 : The tadpole grows into a little froglet in about 12 weeks. It has four legs, and a short tail.
Stage 4 : The lungs begin to work, the gills and tail disappear, and the legs become strong enough to enable itto
hop on land. Finally, in about 14 weeks, a fully grown adult frog hops out from the water.

Specific heat of a substance is defined as the heat required to change the temperature of one gram substan
by 1°C. It is same for increasing or decreasing the temperature of a substance. Here, there is no change in
state of the substance but the temperature of substance changes. :
As said above, normally when heat is given to a substance then its temperature rises v Latent means
however during the state change (from solid to liquid or liquid to gas), there is no rise lying hidden.
in temperature of the substance. The-heat-enerey-which-issupplied ta change the state
of the substance is called latent heat. Latent heat does not change the temperature of the substance.
For more details, it is latent heat because it remains hidden for the substance undergoing the change of stat
and does not show its presence by change in the temperature. In other words, the latent heat which is given
change the state of the substance cannot be detected by a thermometer.
Reason: Every substance (solid or liquid) has some force of attraction between its particles which hold th
together. Now if a substance has to change its state, then it is necessary for it to overcome or break these
forces of attraction between its particles. Thus, the latent heat which is supplied is used up in overcoming
forces of attraction between the particles of a substance during the change of state. The latent heat does
increase the kinetic energy of the particles of that substance and hence due to which there is no rise in the
temperature. Latent heat is of two types:
+ Latent Heat of Fusion : The amount of heat ene; is i S into liquil
atmospheric pressure, at its melting point is known as the latent heat of fusion.
Note : Freezing point ofa liquid is same as the melting point of its solid state. The only difference is
when ice at 0°C melts, it absorbs latent heat of fusion to form water at the same temperature. Whil¢
when water at 0°C freezes to form ice at same temperature then it gives out equal amount of heat.

As we look at our surroundings, we see a large variety of things with different shapes, sizes and textures. Everything in this universe is made up of material which scientists have named “matter”. The air we breathe, the food we eat, stones, clouds, stars, plants and animals, even a small drop of water or a particle of sand — every thing is matter. We can also see as we look around that all the things mentioned above occupy space and have mass. In other words, they have both mass* and volume**. Since early times, human beings have been trying to understand their surroundings. Early Indian philosophers classified matter in the form of five basic elements — the “Panch Tatva ” — air, earth, fire, sky and water. According to them everything, living or non- living, was made up of these five basic elements. Ancient Greek philosophers had arrived at a similar classification of matter. Modern day scientists have evolved two types of classification of matter based on their physical properties and chemical nature. In this chapter we shall learn about matter based on its physical properties. Chemical aspects of matter will be taken up in subsequent chapters. 1.1 Physical Nature of Matter 1.1.1 M ATTER IS MADE UP OF PARTICLES For a long time, two schools of thought prevailed regarding the nature of matter. One school believed matter to be continuous like a block of wood, whereas, the other thought that matter was made up of particles like sand. [I Plasma Membrane or Cell Membrane
This is the outermost covering of the cell that separates the contents of the cell from its external environment
The plasma membrane is flexible and is made up of organic molecules called lipids and proteins. However, we
can observe the structure of the plasma membrane only through an electron microscope. The plasma membrane
al allows or permits the entry and exit of some materials in and out of the cell. It also prevents movement of some
other materialy The cell membrane, therefore, is/called a selectively permeable membrane. Movement of ~
substances through cell occurs through the following ways:
There is spontaneous movement of a substance (solid, liquid, gas) from a region of high concentration to a
2 region where its concentration is low.
Water also obeys the law of diffusion. The movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable
~ membrane (a porous surface that allows only selective particles to pass through) is called osmosis, In osmosis,
water moves from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.

mouth, foot, head, arms, legs, etc.

from one place to another is called locomotion.

After some time you can see Car | change its position from A to B. So, for you, the car is in motion

Suppose there is another car (Car 2), parked on the roadside. You cannot see any change in its position after
some time. Therefore, for you, Car 2 is not moving on road, the trees or the buildings around you are also
at rest. We, therefore, say that an object is in motion if its position changes with time (such as Car 1) in

relation to a stationary object such as a building or a tree, and an object is at rest if its position does not

change with time (such as Car 2) in relation to a stationery object

questions.question_text: What is the primary purpose of an itinerary?
questions.option_a: To provide a detailed plan for a trip or event.
questions.option_b: To list all the expenses of a trip.
questions.option_c: To serve as a souvenir of a trip.
questions.option_d: To record the weather conditions during a trip.

questions.question_text: Which of the following elements is LEAST likely to be found in a typical itinerary?
questions.option_a: Transportation details (flights, trains, etc.)
questions.option_b: Packing recommendations based on weather forecasts
questions.option_c: Scheduled activities and appointments.
questions.option_d: Contact information for hotels and tour operators.

questions.question_text: An itinerary specifies a 'meet-up point' described as 'GPS coordinates: 34.0522° N, 118.2437° W; Landmark: Southwest corner of the Grand Central Market food hall'. What aspect of itinerary creation does this BEST exemplify?
questions.option_a: Use of universally accepted time zones.
questions.option_b: Emphasis on vague and flexible arrangements.
questions.option_c: Combining absolute location data with readily identifiable landmarks.
questions.option_d: Prioritizing budget-friendly accommodation options.

questions.question_text: What is the first operation you should perform in the expression: 12 + (18 ÷ 3) × 2 - 5?
questions.option_a: Addition
questions.option_b: Division
questions.option_c: Multiplication
questions.option_d: Subtraction

questions.question_text: Which expression will give the largest answer?
What is the value of: 100 ÷ (2 × 5) + 3?
Which of the following expressions is equal to 14?
What is the first step you should take when solving the following equation: 12 + (18 - 6) × 2 ÷ 3?
questions.option_a: Addition (12 + 18)
questions.option_b: Subtraction (18 - 6)
questions.option_c: Multiplication (6 × 2)
questions.option_d: Division (2 ÷ 3)

questions.question_text: Which of the following expressions will result in the largest value?
If you change the position of the brackets in the expression 10 + 5 × 2, how many different answers can you get?
Which operation should be performed last in the expression: 36 - 4 × (8 ÷ 2) + 5?
questions.option_a: Subtraction
questions.option_b: Multiplication
questions.option_c: Division
questions.option_d: Addition

questions.question_text: Based on the provided text, which of the following innovations had the MOST significant impact on the development of new modes of transport, moving beyond animal and water-based methods?
questions.option_a: The creation of hollow cavities in logs for boats.
questions.option_b: The invention and improvement of the wheel.
questions.option_c: The use of animals to pull carts.
questions.option_d: The invention of the steam engine.

questions.question_text: The text describes an experiment tracking an ant's movement by marking its position at intervals. If you marked an ant's position every 3 seconds for a minute and then connected the marks, what would the resulting pattern most effectively demonstrate?
questions.option_a: The ant's preferred food source on the paper.
questions.option_b: The ant's average speed throughout the minute.
questions.option_c: The change in the ant's position over time, illustrating motion.
questions.option_d: The total distance the ant traveled in a straight line.

questions.question_text: If a student wants to test if light is necessary for seed germination, which two pots should they compare from the experiment?
questions.option_a: Pot A and Pot B
questions.option_b: Pot B and Pot D
questions.option_c: Pot C and Pot D
questions.option_d: Pot A and Pot C

questions.question_text: The experiment describes 'Reproduction' as the process of producing new ones of one's own kind. Why is this process considered 'necessary for the continuity of life'?
questions.option_a: Because it makes organisms grow bigger and stronger.
questions.option_b: Because it allows individual organisms to live longer.
questions.option_c: Because it ensures that new generations replace older ones, preventing extinction.
questions.option_d: Because it helps organisms adapt to different environments.

questions.question_text: Pot B has 'excess water' such that water is always present above the soil. What problem might this cause for seed germination, even if other conditions are met?
questions.option_a: The seeds might get too much sunlight and burn.
questions.option_b: The seeds might not get enough air, which is needed for respiration.
questions.option_c: The seeds might become too cold and stop growing.
questions.option_d: The seeds might float away and not be able to root.

questions.question_text: Robert Hooke observed 'little rooms' in a cork slice using a primitive microscope. What was the most significant limitation of his observation compared to Anton Van Leeuwenhoek's later discoveries?
questions.option_a: Hooke could not see the nucleus within the cells.
questions.option_b: Hooke only observed dead plant cells, not living organisms.
questions.option_c: Hooke's microscope was unable to magnify objects sufficiently.
questions.option_d: Hooke incorrectly identified the 'little rooms' as cells.

questions.question_text: The 'old cell theory' stated that all plants and animals are composed of cells and that the cell is the basic unit of life. How did Rudolf Virchow's contribution further expand this theory?
questions.option_a: He discovered that cells contain a fluid substance called protoplasm.
questions.option_b: He identified the nucleus as a prominent organelle within the cell.
questions.option_c: He proposed that all cells originate from pre-existing cells.
questions.option_d: He observed the first free-living cells in pond water.

questions.question_text: During the onion peel observation activity, what is the primary purpose of placing the onion peel in a watch glass containing water before transferring it to the slide?
questions.option_a: To stain the cells so they are easier to see under the microscope.
questions.option_b: To prevent the peel from drying out and to keep it from folding.
questions.option_c: To clean the peel of any impurities before observation.
questions.option_d: To make the cell wall more rigid for better viewing.

questions.question_text: If you observe an onion cell under a compound microscope, which of the following structures would you expect to see that is NOT typically found in an animal cell?
questions.option_a: A prominent nucleus.
questions.option_b: A rigid cell wall surrounding the cell membrane.
questions.option_c: Large vacuoles within the cell.
questions.option_d: Both B and C.

questions.question_text: Before a cell divides, how does the chromatin material organize itself?
questions.option_a: It remains as an entangled mass of thread-like structures.
questions.option_b: It disappears completely.
questions.option_c: It gets organized into chromosomes.
questions.option_d: It forms a nucleoid.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a key difference between prokaryotes and eukaryotes regarding their genetic material?
questions.option_a: Prokaryotes have their genetic material inside a well-defined nucleus, while eukaryotes do not.
questions.option_b: Eukaryotes have an undefined nuclear region called a nucleoid, while prokaryotes have a true nucleus.
questions.option_c: Prokaryotes have an undefined nuclear region containing only nucleic acids, while eukaryotes have genetic material inside a well-defined nucleus.
questions.option_d: Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes have their genetic material exposed in the cytoplasm.

questions.question_text: Based on the information provided, what does the term 'karyon' refer to in the words 'prokaryote' and 'eukaryote'?
questions.option_a: Primitive
questions.option_b: True
questions.option_c: Nucleus
questions.option_d: Cell membrane

questions.question_text: If a cell is described as having 'membrane-bound cell organelles', what type of cell is it most likely to be?
questions.option_a: Prokaryotic
questions.option_b: Eukaryotic
questions.option_c: Bacterial
questions.option_d: A cell without a nucleus

questions.question_text: A student observes a container of stagnant water and finds small, worm-like creatures swimming in it. Based on the mosquito life cycle described, which two distinct life stages could these creatures represent?
questions.option_a: Egg and adult mosquito
questions.option_b: Larva and pupa
questions.option_c: Pupa and adult mosquito
questions.option_d: Adult mosquito and egg

questions.question_text: If a community implements a campaign to cover all water tanks and regularly empty containers that can hold water, which stage of the mosquito life cycle would be most directly impacted and why?
questions.option_a: The adult stage, by preventing them from flying.
questions.option_b: The egg stage, by removing the places where female mosquitoes lay eggs.
questions.option_c: The pupa stage, by making it difficult for them to emerge.
questions.option_d: The larva stage, by suffocating them in covered tanks.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements accurately describes why mosquito larvae can breathe underwater?
questions.option_a: They have gills that extract oxygen from the water.
questions.option_b: They absorb oxygen directly through their skin.
questions.option_c: They use siphons to reach the water surface for air.
questions.option_d: They have specialized cells that produce oxygen.

questions.question_text: A passenger inside a bus sees their fellow passengers as being at rest. However, a person standing on the roadside sees the bus and its passengers as moving. This observation best illustrates which concept?
questions.option_a: The law of universal gravitation.
questions.option_b: Motion is a relative term.
questions.option_c: Objects always move in a straight line.
questions.option_d: All objects are constantly in motion.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scenarios best represents a combination of rotatory motion and non-periodic motion?
questions.option_a: A ceiling fan rotating at a constant speed.
questions.option_b: A potter's wheel spinning and then gradually slowing down and stopping.
questions.option_c: A pendulum swinging back and forth with a consistent rhythm.
questions.option_d: A car driving in a straight line on a highway.

questions.question_text: A car travels 5 km north, then turns around and travels 3 km south. Which of the following statements is true regarding its distance and displacement?
questions.option_a: Distance = 8 km, Displacement = 8 km
questions.option_b: Distance = 8 km, Displacement = 2 km north
questions.option_c: Distance = 2 km, Displacement = 8 km
questions.option_d: Distance = 2 km, Displacement = 2 km north

questions.question_text: A car travels 10 km north, then turns around and travels 3 km south. Which of the following statements is true about the distance and displacement of the car?
questions.option_a: The distance traveled is 7 km, and the displacement is 7 km north.
questions.option_b: The distance traveled is 13 km, and the displacement is 7 km north.
questions.option_c: The distance traveled is 7 km, and the displacement is 13 km north.
questions.option_d: The distance traveled is 13 km, and the displacement is 13 km north.

questions.question_text: A car travels 100 km in 2 hours. Then, it stops for 30 minutes, and travels another 50 km in 1 hour. What is the average speed of the car for the entire journey?
questions.option_a: 50 km/h
questions.option_b: 40 km/h
questions.option_c: 30 km/h

questions.question_text: Selvi walks a circular path of radius 7 meters and returns to her starting point. Her displacement is zero, but if she then walks 5 meters east, then 4 meters north, and finally 2 meters west, what is her total displacement from her initial starting point (before the circular walk)?
questions.option_a: 5 meters North
questions.option_b: 5 meters East
questions.option_c: 3 meters East and 4 meters North
questions.option_d: 9 meters

questions.question_text: A car travels for 1 hour at 40 km/hr, then for 0.5 hours at 60 km/hr, and finally for 1.5 hours at 30 km/hr. If another car traveled the same total distance in 2.5 hours, what would be its average speed?
questions.option_a: 46 km/hr
questions.option_b: 38.33 km/hr
questions.option_c: 50 km/hr
questions.option_d: 40 km/hr

questions.question_text: A car accelerates from rest to 30 m/s in 5 seconds. What is its acceleration?
questions.option_a: 6 m/s²
questions.option_b: 150 m/s²
questions.option_d: 35 m/s²

questions.question_text: A car increases its speed from 36 km/h to 54 km/h in 10 seconds. What is its acceleration?
questions.option_a: 0.5 m/s²
questions.option_b: 3 m/s²
questions.option_c: 18 m/s²
questions.option_d: 30 m/s²

questions.question_text: A car travels 30 km at a uniform speed of 40 km/h and then another 30 km at a uniform speed of 20 km/h. What is the average speed of the car for the entire journey?
A car travels 100 meters in 10 seconds, then stops for 5 seconds, and then travels another 50 meters in 5 seconds. What is the average speed of the car during its entire journey?
questions.option_a: 10 m/s

questions.question_text: A car is traveling at a constant speed of 50 km/h. Suddenly, the driver applies the brakes, causing the car to slow down to 30 km/h in 5 seconds. Which of the following best describes the car's acceleration during this time?
questions.option_a: The car has positive acceleration because its speed is still positive.
questions.option_b: The car has negative acceleration because its velocity is decreasing.
questions.option_c: The car has zero acceleration because it is still moving forward.
questions.option_d: The car has uniform velocity because it changed speed smoothly.

questions.question_text: A car travels 60 km in the first hour and then 80 km in the second hour. If you want to find the car's average speed, what calculation would you need to perform?
questions.option_a: Add 60 km and 80 km, then divide by 1 hour.
questions.option_b: Multiply 60 km by 80 km, then divide by 2 hours.
questions.option_c: Add 60 km and 80 km, then divide by 2 hours.
questions.option_d: Subtract 60 km from 80 km, then divide by 2 hours.

questions.question_text: A cyclist travels from point A to point B along a circular track with a circumference of 314 m, where AB is the diameter. What is the distance covered by the cyclist?
An auto travels at a rate of 25 km/h for 4 minutes, then at 50 km/h for 8 minutes, and finally at 20 km/h for 2 minutes. What is the total distance covered in this trip?
questions.option_a: 19 km
questions.option_b: 29 km
questions.option_c: 9 km
questions.option_d: 30 km

questions.question_text: A bus starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.1 m/s² for 2 minutes. Which of the following statements is true about its motion?
questions.option_a: The bus will reach a speed of 12 m/s.
questions.option_b: The bus will cover a distance of 1440 meters.
questions.option_c: If the acceleration were doubled, its final speed would be 6 m/s.
questions.option_d: The bus travels at a constant speed during the entire 2 minutes.

questions.question_text: Usha swims in a 90 m long pool. She covers 180 m in one minute by swimming from one end to the other and back along the same straight path. Which of the following statements is true regarding her average speed and average velocity?
questions.option_a: Her average speed is 3 m/s and her average velocity is 0 m/s.
questions.option_b: Her average speed is 0 m/s and her average velocity is 3 m/s.
questions.option_c: Both her average speed and average velocity are 3 m/s.
questions.option_d: Both her average speed and average velocity are 0 m/s.

questions.question_text: According to the text, which of the following is NOT considered matter?
questions.option_a: A drop of water
questions.option_b: The air we breathe
questions.option_c: Sound
questions.option_d: A particle of sand

questions.question_text: What is the primary characteristic that differentiates matter from things like heat or light, according to the provided text?
questions.option_a: Matter can be seen, while heat and light cannot.
questions.option_b: Matter possesses mass and occupies space, unlike heat and light.
questions.option_c: Matter is made of atoms, and heat and light are not.
questions.option_d: Matter can be classified, but heat and light cannot.

questions.question_text: If a new discovery showed a substance that occupies space but has no mass, based on the definition provided, would it be classified as matter?
questions.option_a: Yes, because it occupies space.
questions.option_b: No, because it must possess mass AND occupy space.
questions.option_c: Only if it can be felt by our senses.
questions.option_d: It depends on its origin.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best describes the relationship between atoms and molecules, based on the text?
questions.option_a: Atoms are larger than molecules and contain them.
questions.option_b: Molecules are the building blocks of atoms.
questions.option_c: Atoms are the building blocks of matter, and molecules are the smallest independent particles of matter.
questions.option_d: Atoms and molecules are interchangeable terms for the same particle.

questions.question_text: The ancient Indian philosopher's classification of matter into 'Panchtatva' (air, earth, fire, sky, and water) differs from modern scientific classification by:
questions.option_a: Focusing on living vs. non-living things.
questions.option_b: Classifying matter based on observable properties rather than physical and chemical properties.
questions.option_c: Excluding the concept of atoms and molecules.
questions.option_d: Only considering non-living matter.

questions.question_text: A student performs Activity-1 using a different colored substance. After 7 dilutions, the water is still slightly colored. What can the student confidently conclude about the original substance?
questions.option_a: The substance completely disappeared after the dilutions.
questions.option_b: The substance's particles are extremely small and can divide into even smaller particles.
questions.option_c: The substance reacted with the water to form a new, colorless compound.
questions.option_d: The student made an error in the dilution process, as the color should have vanished.

questions.question_text: If a scientist observes a substance that can be easily broken down into its components by a simple physical process, what can be definitively said about that substance according to the definition provided?
questions.option_a: It is a pure element.
questions.option_b: It is a mixture, not a substance.
questions.option_c: It has a specific composition and specific properties.
questions.option_d: It is made of particles that cannot be seen.

questions.question_text: Activity-2 demonstrates the diffusion of liquids with different densities. If a liquid diffuses very quickly in water, what can be inferred about its density compared to honey?
questions.option_a: Its density is much higher than honey's.
questions.option_b: Its density is similar to honey's.
questions.option_c: Its density is lower than honey's.
questions.option_d: Density has no impact on the rate of diffusion.

questions.question_text: Robert Brown's observation of pollen grains moving irregularly in water provides strong evidence for what concept?
questions.option_a: The ability of water to dissolve various substances.
questions.option_b: The continuous and irregular movement of particles in liquids.
questions.option_c: The process of evaporation and condensation.
questions.option_d: The specific composition of substances.

questions.question_text: Imagine you are performing Activity-1. Instead of potassium permanganate, you use a substance that, after 5 dilutions, the color completely disappears. What could be a plausible reason for this observation based on the provided text?
questions.option_a: The substance's particles are larger and do not divide as much as potassium permanganate particles.
questions.option_b: The substance is actually a mixture, not a true substance.
questions.option_c: The substance has a very high density, preventing further diffusion.
questions.option_d: The water used for dilution was contaminated.

questions.question_text: A student observes dust particles moving randomly in a beam of sunlight. Based on the provided text, what two fundamental conclusions about matter can be drawn from this observation?
questions.option_a: Matter is made of tiny particles, and these particles are constantly moving.
questions.option_b: Dust particles are alive, and they produce their own energy to move.
questions.option_c: Light energy directly causes dust particles to move in a zig-zag pattern.
questions.option_d: Only dust particles exhibit Brownian motion; other matter does not.

questions.question_text: In the sugar dissolution experiment, why does the sugar solution's volume remain the same as the initial water level, even after adding 50g of sugar?
questions.option_a: The sugar particles evaporate as soon as they are added to the water.
questions.option_b: The sugar particles are too heavy to affect the water's volume.
questions.option_c: The sugar particles occupy the spaces between the water molecules.
questions.option_d: The water molecules expand to accommodate the sugar particles.

questions.question_text: If you were to repeat Activity-3 (potassium permanganate dilution) with very cold water instead of room temperature water, what might you observe regarding the color spread in the subsequent beakers, and why?
questions.option_a: The color would spread faster because cold water molecules move more rapidly.
questions.option_b: The color would spread slower because the kinetic energy of particles decreases with lower temperature.
questions.option_c: The color intensity would be much darker in all beakers due to the cold.
questions.option_d: There would be no change in the rate of color spread, as temperature does not affect particle movement.

questions.question_text: Based on the incense stick activity (Activity-4), which statement best explains why the smell of a lit incense stick can be detected from a distance more easily than an unlit one?
questions.option_a: Burning incense produces larger scent particles that travel further.
questions.option_b: The heat from the burning incense increases the kinetic energy of the scent particles, causing them to move faster and spread out.
questions.option_c: Unlit incense sticks do not release any scent particles into the air.
questions.option_d: The smoke from the lit incense stick carries the scent particles directly to the nose.

questions.question_text: The text states that Brownian motion increases on increasing the temperature. Given this, what would you expect to happen to the movement of dust particles in a beam of light if the room temperature significantly decreased?
questions.option_a: The dust particles would move faster and more erratically.
questions.option_b: The dust particles would stop moving entirely.
questions.option_c: The dust particles would move slower and less frequently.
questions.option_d: The size of the dust particles would increase, making them more visible.

questions.question_text: A chef notices that the aroma of hot soup fills the kitchen much faster than the smell of a cold salad. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?
questions.option_a: Hot soup particles have stronger cohesive forces.
questions.option_b: The particles in hot soup have more kinetic energy and diffuse faster.
questions.option_c: Cold salad particles have more adhesive force with air.
questions.option_d: Diffusion only occurs with liquids, not solids.

questions.question_text: The text describes the Agariyas' traditional practice of salt farming. What extreme environmental condition do they endure for eight months to produce salt from seawater?
questions.option_a: Extreme cold
questions.option_b: Extreme humidity
questions.option_c: Extreme heat of the desert
questions.option_d: Extreme rainfall

questions.question_text: Imagine you have a piece of chalk, a block of ice, and an iron nail. If you try to break each with a hammer, which one would require the most force to break, and why?
questions.option_a: Chalk, because its particles have weak cohesive forces.
questions.option_b: Ice, because its particles are held together by strong adhesive forces.
questions.option_c: Iron nail, because the attractive forces between its particles are very strong.
questions.option_d: All would break with the same force because they are all matter.

questions.question_text: You've left a drawing on a classroom blackboard with chalk for several weeks, and now it's very difficult to erase. What scientific principle explains why the chalk has become so hard to remove?
questions.option_a: Cohesive forces between chalk particles have increased over time.
questions.option_b: The chalk particles have diffused into the blackboard's surface.
questions.option_c: The blackboard has developed stronger adhesive forces with the chalk.
questions.option_d: The temperature of the classroom caused the chalk to solidify.

questions.question_text: If you open a bottle of perfume in one corner of a large room, the fragrance eventually spreads throughout the entire room. This is an example of diffusion. What would happen to the rate at which the fragrance spreads if the room's temperature were significantly increased?
questions.option_a: The fragrance would spread slower because particles would lose energy.
questions.option_b: The fragrance would spread at the same rate, as temperature doesn't affect diffusion.
questions.option_c: The fragrance would spread faster because the particles would move with more energy.
questions.option_d: The fragrance would not spread at all if the temperature increased too much.

questions.question_text: Which of the following scenarios primarily demonstrates cohesive force, as opposed to adhesive force or diffusion?
questions.option_a: Paint sticking to a wall.
questions.option_b: Water molecules forming a droplet on a leaf.
questions.option_c: The smell of baking cookies spreading through a house.
questions.option_d: Sugar dissolving in water.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains why gases are used in applications like LPG cylinders, oxygen tanks, and CNG vehicles?
questions.option_a: Gases are highly compressible, allowing a large amount to be stored in a small space.
questions.option_b: Gases are less dense than liquids, making them easier to transport.
questions.option_c: Gases are always in a gaseous state at room temperature.
questions.option_d: Gases are excellent conductors of heat and electricity.

questions.question_text: A substance is described as a 'vapour' rather than a 'gas' if it:
questions.option_a: Exists in a gaseous state at room temperature.
questions.option_b: Exists in solid or liquid form at room temperature but can become a gas.
questions.option_c: Is highly compressible and used as fuel.
questions.option_d: Is a mixture of ionized particles.

questions.question_text: Plasma, the fourth state of matter, is characterized by:
questions.option_a: Particles that are extremely cold and have very low density.
questions.option_b: Super energetic and super excited particles in the form of ionized gases.
questions.option_c: Rigid particles that maintain their shape regardless of the container.
questions.option_d: Particles that flow easily and take the shape of their container.

questions.question_text: If you observe a fluorescent tube glowing, what state of matter is primarily responsible for this phenomenon?
questions.option_a: Solid, due to the glass of the tube.
questions.option_b: Liquid, formed by the condensation inside the tube.
questions.option_c: Plasma, created by the ionization of gas within the tube.
questions.option_d: Bose-Einstein Condensate, due to extremely low temperatures.

questions.question_text: The Bose-Einstein Condensate is formed by:
questions.option_a: Heating a gas to extremely high temperatures until it ionizes.
questions.option_b: Cooling a gas of very low density to super low temperatures.
questions.option_c: Compressing a gas until it becomes a liquid.
questions.option_d: Mixing different types of gases together at room temperature.

questions.question_text: A chef is trying to boil water at a very high altitude where atmospheric pressure is much lower than at sea level. How would this affect the boiling point of the water compared to boiling water at sea level?
questions.option_a: The water would boil at a higher temperature.

questions.option_c: The 'Panch Tatva' directly corresponds to the five states of matter identified by modern science, indicating a strong foundational agreement across different eras.

questions.question_text: Activity 1.1 demonstrates that when salt dissolves in water, the water level does not significantly change. Based on this observation and the provided explanation, what can be inferred about the arrangement and interaction of particles in a solution?

questions.option_b: Water particles are continuous and do not have any spaces for other substances to occupy.
questions.option_c: The particles of salt are much smaller than water particles and fit into the intermolecular spaces within the water, indicating matter is particulate and not continuous.
questions.option_d: The dissolution process involves a chemical reaction that reduces the overall volume of the mixture.

questions.question_text: The text states that modern scientists classify matter based on 'physical properties and chemical nature.' Given that this chapter will focus on physical properties, what specific aspect of matter's physical nature is being explored through activities like dissolving salt in water?

questions.question_text: Based on Activity 1.4, which observation would most effectively demonstrate the continuous movement of particles and the influence of intermolecular forces, considering the spreading rates of ink and honey in water?
questions.option_a: The immediate dispersion of ink compared to the slow diffusion of honey, indicating differences in particle size and viscosity.
questions.option_b: The eventual even distribution of both ink and honey, confirming that all particles are in constant motion regardless of their nature.
questions.option_c: The observation that ink spreads faster in hot water than in cold water, while honey's rate remains largely unaffected by temperature.
questions.option_d: The color of ink becoming lighter with each dilution, whereas honey's color intensity persists, revealing variations in molecular structure.

questions.question_text: Activity 1.5 demonstrates that the rate of mixing changes with temperature. If a crystal of potassium permanganate is dropped into water at 0°C and another into water at 100°C, what would be the most significant difference observed in the mixing process, and why?
questions.option_a: The crystal in 0°C water would dissolve much faster due to increased solvent density, while the crystal in 100°C water would remain undissolved for longer.
questions.option_b: The crystal in 100°C water would mix significantly faster because higher temperature increases the kinetic energy of water particles, leading to more frequent and energetic collisions with the crystal's particles.
questions.option_c: Both crystals would mix at the same rate, as temperature primarily affects the state of matter of water, not the rate of particle diffusion.
questions.option_d: The crystal in 0°C water would show a more vibrant color diffusion due to the lower kinetic energy allowing for more concentrated particle distribution before spreading.

questions.question_text: The experiment with potassium permanganate dilution suggests that even after 5 to 8 dilutions, the color is still visible. What fundamental characteristic of matter does this observation most strongly support?
questions.option_a: Particles of matter have spaces between them, allowing for even distribution during dilution.

questions.option_d: Particles of matter exhibit strong intermolecular forces, which prevents them from completely disappearing even after repeated dilutions.

questions.question_text: A student observes a rubber band, sugar crystals, and a sponge. Based on the provided text, which of the following statements most accurately explains why all three are considered solids despite exhibiting varied behaviors under external forces?

questions.option_b: They are all rigid and incompressible, and any perceived change in shape is merely an illusion caused by their molecular structure.
questions.option_c: Their ability to regain original shape after force application, or the fixed shape of their constituent particles, defines them as solids, regardless of their bulk form.
questions.option_d: The primary characteristic of a solid is its inability to flow, which is true for all three examples, despite other differences in their physical properties.

questions.question_text: Considering the properties of solids and liquids described, which of the following scenarios best illustrates the diffusion of solids and gases into liquids, and its biological significance?
questions.option_a: A sugar cube dissolving in hot tea, demonstrating that solids can only diffuse into liquids at elevated temperatures, which is irrelevant to aquatic life.
questions.option_b: Oxygen and carbon dioxide from the atmosphere dissolving in water, enabling aquatic organisms to respire and photosynthesize, while also allowing some solid nutrients to slowly dissolve in the water.
questions.option_c: A block of ice melting into water, showing a phase change rather than diffusion, and a carbonated drink releasing gas, which is an artificial process.
questions.option_d: Pollutants from industrial waste dissolving in a river, highlighting the negative impact of diffusion without any significant biological advantage.

questions.question_text: The text states that liquids have no fixed shape but a fixed volume, and they can flow. Which of the following conclusions can be logically drawn regarding the arrangement and interaction of particles in a liquid, based on these observed macroscopic properties?
questions.option_a: Liquid particles are tightly packed and held in fixed positions, allowing them to maintain a definite volume but not a definite shape.
questions.option_b: Liquid particles are far apart and move randomly at high speeds, enabling them to take the shape of any container and flow easily.
questions.option_c: Liquid particles are closely packed but can move past one another, allowing for a fixed volume and the ability to conform to the shape of their container while flowing.
questions.option_d: Liquid particles are completely independent of each other, resulting in both an indefinite shape and an indefinite volume, contrary to textual claims.

questions.question_text: Considering the concept of density (mass/volume), and knowing that ice floats on water, what complex relationship must exist between the molecular arrangement of water in its solid and liquid states to account for this anomalous behavior, given that most substances are denser in their solid form?

questions.option_b: The hydrogen bonding in ice creates a more open, crystalline structure, increasing its volume relative to the same mass of liquid water.
questions.option_c: Ice has a higher mass but a disproportionately larger volume compared to liquid water due to strong covalent bonds.
questions.option_d: The kinetic energy of water molecules decreases significantly upon freezing, causing them to repel each other more strongly.

questions.question_text: If a gas completely fills its container and exerts pressure on its walls, what fundamental characteristic of gas particles, when compared to liquids and solids, is primarily responsible for this behavior, and how does this relate to their kinetic energy?
questions.option_a: Gas particles have negligible kinetic energy, causing them to settle at the bottom of the container and exert pressure.
questions.option_b: Gas particles possess high kinetic energy and weak intermolecular forces, allowing them to move freely and collide with container walls.
questions.option_c: Gas particles are incompressible, leading to constant collisions and pressure generation within a confined space.
questions.option_d: The rigidity of gas particles prevents them from settling, ensuring uniform distribution and pressure throughout the container.

questions.option_a: During the conversion of ice to water, due to latent heat of fusion.

questions.option_b: Particles in ice at 0°C have more energy due to their fixed positions, and the ice will immediately convert to steam.
questions.option_c: Both samples have the same energy content since they are at the same temperature, and both will begin to boil simultaneously.
questions.option_d: Particles in ice at 0°C have more kinetic energy, causing it to melt faster than the water can absorb heat.

questions.question_text: The latent heat of vaporisation for water is the amount of heat energy required to change 1 kg of liquid water into steam at atmospheric pressure at its boiling point. How does the energy of particles in steam at 373 K compare to the energy of particles in water at 373 K, and what is the underlying reason for this difference?
questions.option_a: Particles in steam have absorbed extra energy in the form of latent heat of vaporisation, making them possess more energy than water particles at the same temperature.
questions.option_b: Particles in water have a higher kinetic energy at 373 K, allowing them to overcome forces of attraction more effectively than steam particles.
questions.option_c: Both steam and water particles at 373 K possess the same amount of energy because they are at the same temperature, and latent heat is only relevant during phase change.
questions.option_d: Particles in steam have less energy because the conversion from liquid to gas requires energy expenditure, reducing their overall energy content.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements BEST describes the primary function of cartilage in the human body, based on the provided text?

questions.option_b: It is a rigid structure that forms the main framework of the skeleton, like the bones of the arms and legs.
questions.option_c: It connects bones to muscles, allowing for movement through strong fibrous attachments.
questions.option_d: It is responsible for the direct movement of bones by contracting and relaxing in pairs.

questions.question_text: If a person is able to bend their ear, it is primarily due to the presence of which type of tissue?
questions.option_a: Bone tissue, which is flexible in certain areas.
questions.option_b: Tendon tissue, which connects the ear to the skull.
questions.option_c: Cartilage tissue, known for its soft and elastic properties.
questions.option_d: Muscle tissue, which allows for bending movements.

questions.question_text: Consider the movement of your arm. When you raise your arm, what is the most accurate description of the muscle action according to the text?
questions.option_a: The triceps contract to pull the arm up, while the biceps relax.
questions.option_b: Both the biceps and triceps contract simultaneously to lift the arm.
questions.option_c: The biceps contract, becoming shorter and fatter, to pull the arm up, while the triceps relax.
questions.option_d: Muscles push the bones to move the arm upwards.

questions.question_text: Based on the information provided, why are a pair of muscles, like the biceps and triceps, necessary for moving a bone in two directions?
questions.option_a: Because muscles can only contract and pull, not push, requiring opposing muscles for reverse movement.
questions.option_b: Because one muscle provides the initial pull, and the other stabilizes the bone.
questions.option_c: Because tendons can only attach to one muscle at a time, so two are needed for full range of motion.
questions.option_d: Because bones are too heavy for a single muscle to move effectively.
